title: Three Checks to Make Before Buying Property
description: A practical starting point: who can sell it, what you can do with it, and whether it works for your life and budget.
sections: Start with the decision you are actually making

A property purchase often begins with a photograph, a price or a location pin. Turn that first impression into three separate questions: who has the right to sell this property, what use and development are permitted, and whether it suits your purpose at a cost you can manage. These checks apply to the exact parcel or unit, rather than a project name in general.

Write down whether you plan to live there, build later or hold it for another purpose. Your intended use changes the questions you need answered. A weekend destination, for example, may involve very different access and service needs from a primary home.
1. Establish ownership and authority

Request the current deed and the earlier documents that explain the ownership chain. Compare names, survey references, plot details and boundaries. Ask who will sign and receive payment, especially where there are co-owners, inherited interests, a company or a power of attorney.

Use an independent property lawyer to decide which searches and supporting documents are required. An encumbrance certificate and revenue record can help the investigation, but neither is a complete answer on its own. If a discrepancy appears, record it and ask what evidence will resolve it.
2. Confirm approvals and permitted use

Compare the approved layout or building plan with the advertised property. Check the issuing authority, reference, date, survey numbers and conditions. Where RERA registration applies, compare official disclosures with the promoter, location and phase being offered.

Do not assume that a registered sale, residential-looking brochure or marked plot gives permission for any building. Confirm the land use and the permissions your intended construction needs. Keep promised future approvals separate from documents that have already been issued.
3. Test practical fit and total cost

Visit the exact site and travel the route you would actually use. Check access, water, drainage, electricity, neighbouring activity and maintenance arrangements. Put existing facilities and proposed works in different columns.

Request an itemized quotation and allow for applicable transaction charges, professional checks, finance costs and services or construction still to be arranged. The right shortlist is one whose legal, practical and budget questions can all be answered.
Before the first payment

Keep a one-page decision record: documents received, unresolved issues, responsible person and response deadline. Obtain the draft terms and understand cancellation and refund conditions before paying. If someone pressures you to pay while basic information is missing, pause and resolve the gaps.
Use the free handbook to prepare the conversation. It is a general organizing tool; the final review must fit the property and your circumstances.

title: How to Choose a Property Location Beyond the Map Pin
description: A practical method for comparing routes, services, neighbourhood conditions and proposed infrastructure.
sections: Define what the location needs to do

The best location starts with the buyer, not a universal list of famous neighbourhoods. Write down the places you need to reach, how often you travel, who will live there and when you expect to use the property. Separate essential requirements from preferences.

A family living there every day may place schools, healthcare and commuting first. Someone buying a plot to build later still needs to understand current access, services and holding costs. Compare each candidate against the same requirements.
Test the journey from the actual entrance

Use the exact entrance as your starting point. A straight-line distance can hide a long diversion, unsuitable road or restricted access. Record the route, time of day and travel time to each essential destination. Try an alternative route where available.

Observe the last part of the journey as carefully as the main highway. Ask whether legal access is documented, who maintains the connecting road and whether the route remains usable in wet weather. A visible track is not enough to establish an access right.
Check services and site conditions

Ask how water reaches the property, whether individual electricity connections are available and where drainage flows. Find out who supplies and maintains these services and what you will pay. A pipeline or transformer on site may represent only one stage of the work.

Look at neighbouring occupation, traffic, noise, lighting and low areas. Visit at different times where possible. If flood, slope, soil or coastal conditions raise concerns, get an appropriate technical assessment rather than relying on a short sales visit.
Separate present value from future proposals

Create two columns: available now and proposed. For a new airport, highway or commercial centre, record an official source, location, current status and any confirmed access arrangement. If a completion date cannot be verified, leave it unconfirmed.

Test whether you would still consider the property if the proposed work took longer than expected. Future infrastructure can inform a decision, but it should not carry the entire case for a purchase or be treated as a guarantee of resale value.
Build a useful comparison

Score each location consistently for essential travel, legal access, services, site conditions and affordability. Choose your own priorities and keep a serious unresolved legal or technical issue outside the score; a high average cannot cancel it.
Use the downloadable scorecard for two or three shortlisted locations. Add dates and evidence beside observations so the comparison remains useful after the excitement of a site visit has passed.

title: What an Encumbrance Certificate Can - and Cannot - Tell You
description: Understand an EC as one part of a property investigation, including search periods, parcel details and nil results.
sections: Read the certificate as a search result

An encumbrance certificate is useful because it can show registered transactions found for a property within the requested search period. The Andhra Pradesh government property FAQ explains that registered deeds are indexed and the indexing is used to generate the EC. It also explains the issue of a nil certificate where no registered transactions are found.

That makes the search details important. Check the period, registration office and property description. A certificate for a different parcel, an incomplete period or an inconsistent description may not answer your question.
Compare entries with the ownership documents

Arrange the listed transfers and other entries in order and compare them with the deeds supplied by the seller. Ask your lawyer to explain a mortgage, release, unexpected name or missing transfer. Do not assume that every entry is harmless or that an omitted entry proves nothing happened.

Where the record is unclear, request clarification or the appropriate certified records from the registration office. Let the property history guide the search period rather than applying a fixed number of years to every purchase.
A nil result has limits

A nil EC is not a general certificate that every possible ownership or possession issue has been eliminated. It reports the outcome of the relevant registered-record search. Other claims, disputes, errors or matters outside the search need separate attention.

Continue checking the title chain, seller authority, physical possession, boundaries and relevant restrictions. Keep an explanation of each unresolved item with the documents. The goal is a coherent property history, not merely collecting a reassuring-looking certificate.
Use official channels and keep evidence

Use the official registration service or the appropriate registration office. Confirm whether the version you obtain is suitable for your intended purpose and retain its reference and date. Do not send sensitive property or identity information to a website simply because its name resembles an official portal.

Give the certificate and underlying documents to your independent adviser before committing. A broker or seller can help obtain records, but your review should assess your own risks and the exact transaction.
Questions to take to your lawyer

Ask whether the search identifies the correct property, what period is appropriate, whether entries match the deeds, and which further searches or documents are needed. Ask for a clear explanation of any qualification in the advice.
The Land Documents handbook includes a tracker for these questions. Use it to record what you received and what still needs an answer; it does not replace a title opinion.

title: Layout Approval and RERA Registration: Two Different Checks
description: Why buyers should compare the approved plan and applicable RERA disclosures for the exact phase and plot.
sections: Begin with the exact property

An approval reference is only useful when you can connect it to the property being offered. Ask for the project name, promoter, phase, survey references and plot or unit number. Use the same identifiers in your quotation, document folder and site notes.

A project can contain different phases or parcels. Do not assume that a document displayed for one part automatically covers every plot shown in a presentation. Ask for a written explanation of the scope when the match is unclear.
What the approved plan helps you check

A layout plan can show the approved arrangement of plots, roads, open spaces and other designated areas. Check its issuing authority, reference, date and conditions, then locate your plot and compare its dimensions with the sale plan.

Ask whether later revisions exist and which version applies. If a road, amenity area or plot boundary differs between the brochure and approved drawing, ask for clarification before treating the brochure as a specification.
What RERA disclosures add

Where the RERA framework applies, use the official state regulator to compare the project, promoter, location and registration information. Review the disclosed material and available updates rather than checking only whether a number appears on an advertisement.

Registration and planning permission serve different purposes. Neither removes the need to check title, seller authority and the contract. If registration is not provided, ask for the written basis and obtain advice on applicability rather than accepting an unexplained exemption claim.
Permission to build is another question

Buying a residential plot does not automatically approve your particular house design. Building controls, setbacks, site conditions, service arrangements and applicable permissions still need to be addressed.

If the parcel was used or classified as agricultural land, clarify the current land-use and conversion requirements with the competent authority. Procedures can change, and rules from another state may not fit an Andhra Pradesh property.
Keep a dated verification record

Save the official records you reviewed and write down the date and unanswered questions. If an important permission is only promised, describe it as pending in your comparison and ask what commitment the contract actually makes.
The free documents handbook provides a review checklist. Use it with a lawyer and the relevant local professionals so each document answers a specific question about the property you intend to buy.

title: Property Budgeting: Look Beyond the Advertised Price
description: Build a realistic cost worksheet with transaction charges, services, financing and future works.
sections: Compare the same price basis

Before comparing quotations, check the area unit, area measurement and included items. One square yard equals nine square feet, but the conversion only helps if both quotations use comparable areas. Confirm whether the quoted rate applies to the area described in the transaction documents.

Request a total for the exact property. A headline rate may leave out charges or refer to a different plot, size or payment arrangement. Write down the quotation date and validity so an old offer does not distort your shortlist.
Create four cost groups

Group costs into acquisition, finance, making the property usable, and ongoing ownership. Acquisition can include applicable duties, registration charges and professional checks. Finance may include lender charges and interest. Usability costs may involve services, repairs, site preparation or construction.

Ongoing costs can include maintenance, security, taxes and service bills where applicable. Ask who charges each amount, when it becomes due and what it covers. Verify current statutory charges for your transaction rather than borrowing a rate from an old article.
Check when the money is needed

A total can look affordable while the payment timetable is difficult. Put each obligation beside a date and funding source. Allow for a gap between loan approval and actual disbursement, and clarify any conditions affecting the lender release.

Consider whether a delay in selling another asset, obtaining a connection or beginning construction would change your position. Choose a reserve suited to your commitments; a generic emergency-fund figure cannot account for every household.
Price uncertainty openly

Mark estimates as estimates. If service-connection costs, maintenance or construction quantities are not confirmed, obtain more information instead of treating a blank cell as zero. A contingency can help planning, but it should not hide an unresolved material cost.

For a plot, get a design-based construction estimate that matches local development controls. For a built property, arrange appropriate inspection and price foreseeable repairs. The cheapest purchase can become expensive if these costs are overlooked.
Decide on the whole commitment

Compare the total cost with the location, permitted use and legal review. Avoid using a hoped-for resale price or promise of future returns as the only reason the numbers work. Ask how you would manage if resale took longer or the property generated no income.
Use the budget worksheet in the three-check handbook to prepare your questions. Take transaction-specific financing and tax questions to the appropriate adviser before signing.

title: A Plot Site Visit Checklist That Goes Beyond the Entrance
description: Identify the exact plot, examine access and services, and leave with an evidence-based follow-up list.
sections: Prepare before arriving

Ask for the approved plan, plot number, survey references and available dimensions before your visit. Confirm the entrance and meeting point. List the questions that matter to your use of the property so the visit is more than a tour of the most attractive features.

Bring a way to take dated notes and photographs, observing privacy and access permissions. Do not enter unsafe or restricted areas. A sales representative can show the site; unresolved boundaries or technical conditions need the right independent professional.
Find the actual parcel

Locate the plot on the plan and at the site. Compare its position, adjoining plots, road and marked boundaries with the documents. Ask how the demarcation was established and whether a survey can confirm an unclear measurement.

Observe the land level, slope and visible occupation. If you see fencing, structures or use that is not explained by the documents, ask for a written response. Do not assume that a numbered marker settles ownership or possession.
Follow the services, not just the display

Ask where water comes from, how electricity connections will be arranged and where drains lead. Record whether each service is available, installed but not commissioned, under construction or proposed. These stages can have very different implications for use.

Check the route from the main road and ask who is responsible for its upkeep. If common facilities are included, ask where they are, who can use them and which fees or rules apply. Keep separately operated facilities distinct from internal layout amenities.
Change the time and conditions

A second visit can expose traffic, noise, lighting or access conditions hidden during a scheduled daytime tour. Where seasonal drainage matters, seek appropriate observations and technical advice. Avoid interpreting a dry site on one day as proof of all-weather performance.

Speak respectfully with neighbours where appropriate and compare observations with official or professional evidence. Informal accounts can identify questions worth asking, but they are not certificates of compliance or ownership.
Leave with a short follow-up list

For each unresolved issue, note what evidence is needed, who should provide it and when you will review it. Keep photographs beside their location and date. Separate what you personally observed from what someone told you.

Use the location handbook to compare visits consistently. If the legal access, plot identity or service arrangements remain unclear, pause the decision until the right documents or assessments answer them.
